text: A single neuron draws one straight line through its input space and reports which side a point lies on. That is useful, but most interesting patterns cannot be separated by one line, so the natural next step is to ask many neurons the same question at once and see what their answers add up to.

A layer is a group of neurons that all read the same input vector, each with its own weights and its own bias. Because every neuron computes a dot product with that same input, we can stack their weight vectors as the rows of a single matrix, and then the whole layer becomes one matrix multiplied by the input, plus a vector of biases, followed by the activation applied to every entry. One line of algebra now describes as many neurons as we like.

The shapes are worth tracking carefully, because most bugs in neural network code are shape bugs. If the input has three entries and the layer has four neurons, the weight matrix has four rows, one for each neuron, and three columns, one for each input. The bias has four entries, and so does the output. A useful habit is to read a weight matrix's shape as outputs by inputs, and to check that the inner sizes match before you multiply.

Recall from the lessons on matrices that multiplying by a matrix transforms space, stretching and shearing the whole grid while keeping its lines straight and evenly spaced. A layer does exactly that to its inputs, then adds the bias, which slides the grid, and then the ReLU does something no matrix could do: every coordinate that went negative is pushed to zero, so whole regions of the plane are folded flat onto the axes. A layer is a transformation with a crease in it.

Stacking layers means feeding the output of one layer in as the input of the next. The second layer never sees the raw data; it sees the space after the first layer has stretched and folded it, and a problem that was tangled in the original space may have become one that a few straight lines can separate. A network of several layers is therefore a composition of functions, each one reshaping the space for the one that follows.

Every weight and bias is a parameter the network will learn, and counting them is simple: a layer with n inputs and m neurons has m times n weights plus m biases. In a transformer, every block contains a two-layer network of exactly this kind, applied to each token separately. In the smallest version of GPT-2, it widens each token's vector from seven hundred and sixty-eight numbers to four times as many and then narrows it back again, and those two matrices hold about two thirds of the block's parameters.

So a layer is many neurons sharing one input, written compactly as a matrix, and a network is layers composed one after another. Next we look more closely at the bend itself, and at why a network without it would be no better than a single layer.
